utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I think I said, "Madam Registrar," but -- or -- I didn't say -- I don't remember, but, at least, thank you, Mr. Registrar. I first establish that the accused are not in the courtroom. I remember that yesterday one of the last issues we briefly discussed was their absence or presence. May I take it that each of the three accused has used the opportunity we gave yesterday to be absent today and to proceed, that they agree in us proceeding in their absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, on behalf of Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour on behalf of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will deal with quite a number of housekeeping sessions. The first thing I'd like to do is to deliver a decision. It's the Chamber's decision on the admission into evidence of P2726, P2727, D2030 through D2033, D2036, and D2037, documents which were tendered through Witness Sacic. On the 26th of March, 2010, the Markac Defence tendered documents D2030 through D2033, D2036, and D2037 to challenge the credibility of Witness Sacic. This can be found on transcript pages 28041 through 28044. On the 21st of April, 2010, the Prosecution tendered P2726 and P2727 in order to have a complete record, if the Markac Defence documents are admitted. This can be found at transcript pages 28522 through 28524. P2726, P2727, D2030 through D2033, D2036, and D2037 are OTP statements, parts of OTP suspect interviews, as well as Croatian Official Notes and interviews of Witness Sacic. The Cermak Defence submitted that the only portions of the tendered documents that should be admitted into evidence are those that were put to the witness and that they should only be used for impeachment purposes. The Gotovina Defence also submitted that these statements should only be used for impeachment purposes. All three Defence teams further objected to the admission into evidence of P2726 and P2727. The Prosecution raised no objection to the admission into evidence of the Defence documents and further submitted that all statements being tendered could be used both for impeachment purposes and for the truth of their contents. All of this can be found on transcript pages 28511, 28513, and 28521 through P28524. The Markac Defence tendered D2030 through D2033, D2036, and D2037 to challenge the credibility of Witness Sacic. The Chamber recalls that the parties were informed on the 24th of February 2010 that, in relation to Chamber witnesses, they would be able to - and I quote: "Read into the record portions of previous statements alleged to be inconsistent with any evidence given by the witness during his testimony in order to challenge the witness's credibility." And this can be found at transcript page 27120. In this instance, the Markac Defence did not follow this procedure. In order to create a clear and complete record of the proceedings, the Chamber will, rather than asking the Markac Defence at this stage to read the relevant portions into the record, instead allow it to file those portions of the witness's previous statements that were put to him in court. There is then no need to admit the documents into evidence. Accordingly, the Chamber denies the admission into evidence of D2030 through D2033, D2036, and D2037. Considering that the Prosecution conditionally tendered P2726 and P2727 on the admission into evidence of the Defence documents, their admission into evidence is also denied. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The second item deals with a document marked for identification. D2038, which is the decision for appointment of Zeljko Sacic to assistant minister for the crime police, was tendered by the Markac Defence. An English translation was missing. I do understand that it has now been uploaded. Mr. Registrar, would you link the uploaded English translation to D2038 which was, until now, marked for identification. And since there is an English translation now, nothing opposes admission into evidence, unless any of the parties would have any problems with the translation. D2038, in the absence of any objections, is admitted into evidence. A few - and that's the next item on my agenda - a few translations were recently revised. I give you the numbers. It is P510, P577, P2536, D495, D1476, P2455, P2343, P2386, P2002, P2732, and D787. I note that Mr. Registrar informed me that he had, although a revised translation is there, that he has not yet received P2536 and P2732. Mr. Registrar, could you confirm that you did not receive these two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, hereby I confirm. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was -- P2536, if the Chamber will recall, were two -- was the document where two versions, the originals, were found on the Internet, and those were tendered. After some discussion in court, what -- what we had done is we had sent both of those to CLSS and the -- and requested a translation of one into the other at which case -- in which case CLSS told us they will consider the English one to be the translation and prepare the B/C/S translation of the English -- what they considered English original. Because they had two originals in front of them. We sent it to the Defence, and I think there was some discussion, and Mr. Misetic had an issue with considering the English as the original, so his proposal was to leave the two originals in evidence to which we have no problem. But it was after the Court's instruction that we had sent the matter to CLSS, and that's how they had proceeded. That's the issue with P2536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So for one of the versions we have no translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What from what you tell us, Mr. Misetic, but please correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Hedaraly, it seems that it is a very technical matter for which the parties should be able to find a solution, whatever that solution would be. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's -- that's the official interview note of Mr. Bilobrk. That's the one where we sent the aide-memoire to the court. And there was that agreed issue to be correct. And that just hasn't been done yet, but we should be receiving it, hopefully, later today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

Mr. Registrar, you are hereby granted leave to replace P2732 by a new translation where the one and only difference is the difference which was indicated as agreed upon by the parties in the aide-memoire on the ostavita/postavita matter. utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a few -- a few of these exhibits that are still under discussion because obviously, as the court can imagine, some of these come up as we review the evidence. So these have been sent to the Cermak Defence yesterday. We can go into the details today if we need to, but if we can have a procedure in place for this one and other ones where other translation matters may occur, and then we can discuss with the parties and then submit the matter to Mr. Registrar. And then I don't know what's the best way of moving forward for these issues. I don't think it's worth discussing the details of the translation, discussions we're having in court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, what we are mainly talking about is replacing translations by revised translations. I will deal with that at a later stage. Now, from all of the exhibits I've mentioned, P510 is admitted into evidence; P577 -- no, I'm -- I'm making a mistake. It's all admitted into evidence already. The revised translation of P510 can replace the existing translation. The revised translation of P577 can replace the existing translation. For P2536, we wait until we have now the full information. Mr. Registrar may further replace the existing translations of the following documents by the revised and uploaded translations: D495, D1476, P2455, P2343, P2386, P2002. I think I dealt already with P2732. And for D787, we wait until there's an agreed revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask the same thing for P2343, and P2386. We have been in discussion with the Cermak Defence for P2386; I think we're very close to agreement. And for P2343, we have noticed additional changes that needed to be made, and we sent those to the Defence teams yesterday. So if we can also wait on those to have confirmation on whether those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- those are as well confirmed. Then we can have those linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the leave granted to replace the translation of P2343 and P2386 is withdrawn. And we are awaiting the final green light by the parties for replacement of these translations by the new versions on which the parties would then have agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect with P2343, we have already had a chance to review it last night and we don't have any objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we have not heard from the other parties yet. Once all the parties have looked it, could it be presented to the Chamber in a clear way. I'm -- I'll come back later to that because even new matters may arise in view of translation. It can be that one line or another line which has not caught immense attention, nevertheless, would suffer on some translation flaws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to 2343; just checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The same with Markac Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P2343, which started today as being translated by an old translation, then that old translation leave was granted to replace it by a new translation, which was subsequently withdrawn, and now the final word is that Mr. Registrar is given permission to replace the revised translation of P2343 -- no, now I'm making mistakes. To replace the existing translation of P2343 with the revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just to clarify, with the newest revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With the newest revised translation uploaded. And no party could leave the premises of this Tribunal today unless they have verified in every single -- on every single letter whether what is now uploaded is the newest, freshest, revised translation. I quickly move on to another subject. My next item deals with P2678, the minutes of the 277th closed government session, 5th of October, 1995. The parties were to provide a complete translation of this government session to replace the current translation of P2678. I do understand that a full translation covering the whole of the document is now uploaded. Mr. Registrar, did you receive such a new, complete, 100 percent complete, newest translation of P2678?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I confirm, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that new translation may replace - and you're instructed to replace it - may replace the old translation. The question arises whether the -- the two documents which contain elements of P2678, whether they should remain in evidence, because P2678 is the complete version of what is found in part in -- in D214 and D215. Now, the Chamber prefers to have that in evidence because reference is made to those documents and otherwise one would easily be lost. The only question which then arises, if there's any need to make further changes to that or to the translations. The parties are invited to consider that and to inform the Chamber if there are any wishes there. For reference purposes, D214 and D215 are important. However, for access to the complete record and the translation of it, of the closed government session, P2678 will be guiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did have a discussion with the Markac Defence, and what we had suggested is to have, since the originals in D214 and D215 are there, to simply have the complete translation of that portion linked to D214 and to D215 so that everyone can just have the complete access to the record. And then we have P2678 as the full version. So whatever the witness may had referred to in examination, no one has to go chase around other exhibits. But I don't think that we had discussed it, and there seemed to be agreement on that, just to let the Court know that we had discussed the issue previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, forgive me for not having a clear recollection on what exactly was left out and what was translated and what was not translated. May I take it that where the parties agree that they would upload exactly those portions of the translation of P2678 that would match what we find in D214, and the same for D215, and that Mr. Registrar is granted leave to replace the existing translations by these new translations? Well, they're not actually new translations, but it's just more or less transferring them to -- so that D214 and D215 have the translations to the extent that these are portions of P2678. Yes, I said earlier that I would come back to any -- how to deal with these kind of translation issues for the near future. Because we -- we're considering that they'll -- there will be no more court hearings, apart from hearings on closing argument. Therefore, instructions to link revised translations to exhibits in e-court will be given informally. As in the past, the parties should approach the Registry, copying Chamber staff, once they have agreed a revised translation. The Chamber will then consider the revised translation and, accordingly, instruct the Registrar informally -- again, copying the parties. The Registry will then, just prior to the issuing of the Judgement, file on the record a list of exhibits for which translation replacement instructions were given informally. So we deal with the matter all in a rather informal way. And at the very end we have a list of what translations were replaced, and that will be a formal document. This is how the Chamber intends to proceed. Any comments, questions, or suggestions? If not, I would like to move on to the next item on my agenda. D2041, which is a map of the Ramljane area which was tendered through witness Balunovic. Inadvertently, this document was not admitted into evidence, whereas there seemed to be no objections of any kind. Therefore, D2041 is admitted into evidence. The next item concerns D986. On the 1st of December in -- let me just check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the 1st of December, 2008, D986 was admitted into evidence, but it had not yet been released in e-court, which only happened later. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was at the time not released in e-court. That happened only at a later stage. And I just simple put this on the record for full transparency. The Registry has informed the parties of this by e-mail of the 20th of May, 2010, and no objections were raised. The relevant documents, which is 1D63-0218, should be linked to D986 in e-court, and the Registrar is instructed to do so. Then we move on. And I'll deliver a decision -- or, rather, the reasons for a decision that are the reasons for the decision on protective measures for Witness CW-4. On the 15th of April, 2010, Witness CW-4 requested to testify in closed session out of fear for the safety of his family in Croatia. The Prosecution, the Gotovina Defence, and the Markac Defence submitted that protective measures could be granted under the Rules. The Cermak Defence initially objected to the request on the ground that the witness had failed to provide the basis of his fear for the safety of his family. After the parties' submissions, Witness CW-4 testified that his family had received threatening phone calls, after which the Cermak Defence withdrew its objection. The Chamber then granted the protective measures of a pseudonym and testimony in closed session. This can all be found on transcript pages 28174 through 28187, and 28339. The Chamber has previously held that the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard can be satisfied by showing, for example, that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. Witness CW-4 testified that his family had received threatening phone calls and that he was afraid they might be harmed by someone who did not find his statements before the Tribunal to be - and I quote - "suitable." Having considered the parties' submissions and on the basis of the witness's testimony, the Chamber found that the witness had demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of his family, should it become shown that he had given evidence before the Tribunal. The Chamber further considered that, in light of the nature of the anticipated evidence of the witness, the only effective way to protect his identity was to hear his testimony in closed session. Accordingly, the Chamber decided to grant the protective measures of a pseudonym and testimony in closed session. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for granting protective measures to Witness CW-4. I would now like to deliver a decision on the Gotovina Defence request for clarification. The Chamber hereby issues its decision on the Gotovina Defence's request for clarification of the Chamber's correspondence with the Republic of Croatia on the 11th of September, 2009. The correspondence relates to the Prosecution's application for an order, pursuant to Rule 54 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, filed on the 13th of June, 2008, and the Chamber's subsequent order of the 16th of September, 2008. As the parties are aware, the Prosecution's Rule 54 bis application is currently being further considered by the Chamber. A decision will be rendered in due course and is expected to be issued before the summer recess. On the 8th of September, the Chamber received a letter from a representative of the Republic of Croatia requesting information about when a decision on the Prosecution's Rule 54 bis application would be rendered or when a hearing with regard to this matter would be scheduled. On the 11th of September 2009, the acting senior Legal Officer of this Chamber responded that the Chamber was in the process of reviewing and considering submissions and reports provided by the Republic of Croatia and the parties but that he could not provide any estimate as to when this review would be completed. As the parties recall, hearings and meetings on the matter were subsequently scheduled and took place in December 2009, as well as in January and February 2010. The acting senior Legal Officer added, in a correspondence, that until a new order would be issued, the Chamber's order of the 16th September 2008 remained in force. On the 13th of October, 2009, the Gotovina Defence requested clarification of the correspondence of 11th of September, 2009, and of the 16th of September, 2008, order. Specifically, the Gotovina Defence inquired whether and to what extent the order was still in force and pursuant to which Rule it had been issued. On the 27th of October, 2009, the Prosecution responded to the request, arguing, firstly, that the Gotovina Defence had no standing to make this request. It further argued that the correspondence in question merely reiterated what was obvious from the face of the order and that the request should therefore be denied. On the 29th of October, 2009, the Gotovina Defence requested leave to reply, which was not granted. With regard to standing, the Chamber has consistently invited all parties to make submissions and to attend hearings with regard to the Prosecution's Rule 54 bis application. In line with this, the Chamber considers that the Gotovina Defence indeed had standing to make the request. The 16th of September, 2008, order granted, in part, a request by the Republic of Croatia, inter alia, to be allowed to further investigate the whereabouts of certain documents that are the subject of the Prosecution's Rule 54 bis application. The decision to grant the request in part and the order to intensify and broaden the investigation and report the results of the investigation to the Chamber and the Prosecution were issued pursuant to Rule 54. This is indicated in the 16th of September, 2008, order itself. The order remains in force in its entirety until it is amended or replaced by another order or decision issued by the Chamber. The Chamber did not set a time-limit on the validity of the order, although it did set a deadline for the Republic of Croatia to report to the Prosecution and the Chamber. The Chamber notes that Croatia has indicated in various filings that, in its view, it has complied with the order; while the Prosecution has made indications that, in its view, Croatia has not done so. The Chamber has understood these indications only as submissions by the Prosecution and by the Republic of Croatia and emphasises that the decision of whether or when the order has been complied with remains solely within the competence of the Chamber. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The next item I would like to deal with is the Gotovina Defence bar table motion. A written decision will follow, but I hereby already announce that items 1 to 13 of Appendix A of Gotovina's 19th of April, 2010, bar table submission are admitted into evidence. The Chamber has also decided not to admit the complete investigative file which relates to item 8. This was proposed by the Prosecution, and it seems that the fact that no other investigation, apart from the one submitted, was performed until 2006 does not seem to be in dispute. But I'm looking at the parties. Mr. Hedaraly, you know what we are talking about. It's the one document which indicates how investigations were initiated but that it only then in 2006 got a follow-up. Both Gotovina Defence and Prosecution, therefore, agree on that no further investigative activity had been undertaken until 2006. That apparently was the issue. And then it started. And then it's -- we have the investigative file which you would like to -- to present. But the Chamber first focuses on what really, at that time, was the issue, is what investigative activity had been developed and that the Prosecution wanted to stress, in relation to item 8, Nikola Subota, that whatever may have happened at the time it then only received a follow-up in 2006. The parties agree on that. Now, in order to -- to accept this stipulation, it's, until now, a stipulation between the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution. Do the other parties want to join in this stipulation that has not such direct effect, I think, on their cases, but ... If so, it will be a stipulation between all parties. Otherwise, it will be a stipulation only between the Gotovina Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's more appropriate between the other two, Your Honour. It's something with which we cannot satisfy ourselves on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I rather hear that from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Than either to suggest that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you would not disagree. You say this is a stipulation which you have not verified and where you take no position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not a party to that stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the same is true for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same applies to Markac Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I take it the way in which I formulated what you stipulate upon, that is, that since the investigative activity as found in item 8 on the Gotovina Defence bar table motion took place, that no follow-up was there until 2006; would that sufficiently formulate the stipulation? I see Mr. Hedaraly nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. I would -- I don't think it's in dispute either that on the 8th of August an investigative judge was on the scene and did an on-site investigation and that after that, until 2006, there was no further investigative steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way you have described it, and I think what -- if Mr. Misetic is referring to what item 8 says, and I don't remember the exact details, but that's why the -- the way that Mr. President has formulated it is satisfactory for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you do not object to what we find in item 8 at this moment. You're not challenging the truth of the content of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now on the record. The next item I would like to deal with is the decision on the Cermak Defence motion to admit into evidence regulations on procedure of the Public Security Service. I will refer to the regulations on procedures of the Public Security Service hereafter as the regulations. On the 26th of March, 2010, the Chamber sought the assistance of the parties by asking whether the regulations mentioned by Witness Sacic could be produced. This can be found at transcript page 27990. On the 20th of April, 2010, the Cermak Defence requested the Chamber to admit the regulations into evidence. The Prosecution responded on the 4th of May, 2010, stating that it did not object to the admission of the regulations and making further remarks about their relevance. According to Rule 89(C) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Chamber may admit any evidence which it deems relevant and of probative value. The regulations expand on the procedure to be followed when performing an on-site investigation with or without an investigating judge. They furnish further detail on the provisions of Article 145(2) of the Croatian Law on Criminal Procedure and outline the required conduct and obligations of the civilian police in the aftermath of a crime and upon learning of a crime. As the regulations were in force in Croatia during the indictment period, they provide the Chamber with additional legislative framework and information which is both reliable and relevant to the Chamber's ability to assess the evidence of numerous witnesses and better understand the evidence concerning events that transpired. In light of the foregoing considerations, the Chamber finds the regulations to be both relevant and of probative value and admits them into evidence. Finally, considering the absence of objections to admission into evidence and that the Chamber itself sought production of the regulations, the Chamber exceptionally allows their admission into evidence at this stage of the proceedings, namely, after the closure of the Cermak Defence's case in-chief. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on the matter. The regulations have not been assigned an exhibit number yet. Mr. Registrar, could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D2146. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was D2146, which I just admitted -- which the Chamber just admitted into evidence. The next item is the Markac Defence bar table submission in relation to Witness Repinc. A spreadsheet of documents was filed on the 9th of June of 2010. There are a total of 92 documents, all of which are referenced in Witness Repinc's expert report, which is D1932. The Prosecution does not object to 89 of the documents. First of all -- Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If it may assist the Court, we've discussed the matter with Mr. Mikulicic, and we will withdraw our objection to the three documents to which we had initially objected. So I thought I would make that clear before the Chamber moves on with its decision, if it may assist to keep matters short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the items was about the -- and that was number 56 on the list. I'll not deal with the -- with numbers 65 and 44, which were the two other ones which were subject of conversations. The only thing we knew, especially in relation to the handwritten document, is that it was received from Mr. Separovic. The Chamber would like to hear whether there is any further information as far as the provenance of document 56 is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have no further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will consider -- we have no problems with 65 and 44 on the list. But this one, number 56, Markac Defence bar table submission, is a report on the completion of tasks for the 21st of August, 1995, a handwritten document with signature of Mr. Zeljko Sacic, and later transcribed and sent to the, I think, General Staff of the HV. The Chamber will consider, further consider, whether it admits this document into evidence. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But with the exception of number 56 on that list, on the bar table submission in relation to Witness Repinc, the Chamber admits the remaining 91 documents into evidence. And we ask the Registrar to announce a range of numbers. Most likely, later this morning, the Chamber will issue its decision on number 56. Perhaps after a very short break. Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit numbers assigned to Markac Defence bar table submission will be in the exhibit range from D2054 throughout and including D2145. D2109 will remain MFI until the Chamber's decision is issued. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The next item on my agenda deals with P1278. I do understand that the Prosecution would like to amend the reference to the document's ID under P1278 in e-court. Mr. Hedaraly, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. As stated in the surrogate sheet, it should V000-0990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it does not change in any way what is in evidence. Any objections? If not, Mr. Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the document ID reference of P1278 with now the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next item is a bar table submission by the Cermak Defence. It's the -- it is a spreadsheet which the Chamber received yesterday, but there are no comments from the OTP on it. And spreadsheets related to bar table submissions should be filed once the OTP has given its comment on it. But I already -- the Chamber would already like to know from the OTP whether there are any objections against admission, apart from what your comments or what your entries on the relevant column would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We will object, Your Honour. If -- if Your Honour wants further submissions on what the objections are, we can be heard, or we can provide them in the comments section or in a brief filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the Chamber would -- would like to hear your submissions on the matter. And, of course, sometimes objections against admissions take the form of challenging the relevance, which is, of course, one of the requirements for admission, that often and is well-placed in the comments category. But, of course, there may be other objections against admission as well, which are of a totally different nature. The Chamber doesn't know yet. And since we have not seen your comments until now, the Chamber would like to hear your submissions on the matter. Are you able to make these submissions orally today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I am not, but Mr. Carrier behind me is, and he could do it right now if it helps the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would like to give an opportunity to Mr. Carrier. These are -- bar table submissions are usually rather complex. So, Mr. Carrier, I take it that we get a clear expose of you what objections either in general terms or on what specific documents are there. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- perhaps I get it on my screen so that I am better able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although not on my screen, I have it before my eyes at this moment. Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The materials that Cermak Defence wish to tender are underlying documents, all of which are of an investigative nature. At this point, the Prosecution is not aware of the outcome of the investigations themselves. And with specific documents, the perpetrators themselves are unknown. Now, clearly, the motion relates to crimes committed by the Serbian military police, paramilitary forces, Serb volunteers, and Serb civilians. This was in their first bar table motion in the Krajina during that period of time. The -- for example, one of the documents, 2D850, is the beginning of an investigation where the perpetrators are unidentified. 2D849, again, unknown perpetrators. 2D844, this one has "probably by local Chetniks." The Prosecution submits that is not sufficiently identifying. 2D845, nothing on the perpetrators. 2D851, again. 2D852. And with regard to some of the other documents, there are very detailed accounts of certain instances of crimes being committed where the Prosecution is not in a position to -- to verify that in order to -- to stipulate to it. So we've maintained throughout this process with regard to these bar table submissions from the Cermak Defence that our preference is that they pick portions of the Martic Judgement that satisfy their needs. And we're more than willing to stipulate to those needs. But with regard to documents that they want to tender that don't identify the perpetrator, obviously that doesn't satisfy their purpose. And with regard to more detailed accounts, we're not a position to stipulate to that. And with these documents in particulars, given that they're investigative documents, the outcome of the investigation we're not aware of. We're not in a position to stipulate on that basis either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before I give you an opportunity to respond, it was my understanding that the purpose of this exercise was primarily to establish that circumstances led at the time the investigative authorities to take action in these periods of time, and not primarily for the Chamber to adopt any conclusions or to evaluate the evidence in there but, rather, to give an overall picture of rather intensive investigative activities, which was related to reports on crimes committed against civilians, Croatian -- Croat civilians. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not just investigative matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is of a general nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On-site investigations go beyond that for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. This goes, as the first bar table did, which didn't receive any objection, to the general information that is available on the issue of why there might be or there could be a revenge motive of individuals because of what happened to them in the previous period of time, between 1991 and 1995. This is not meant to be an exhaustive investigation by us proving each and every crime, which would be simply impossible. We don't have the resources for that. That has never been something ever undertaken. But it goes to a relevant issue in the case as to the existence of individuals, because of what happened to them, committing attacks back and not being part of a criminal plan. Now, the history of this goes back to one of late and wrong -- failure -- or a failure to disclose Rule 68 material, which required litigation and required us to sort this matter out during the currency of the trial. We submitted this bar table on the 15th of April, 2010, and we've received nothing back since that time. In our submission, this information contains the kind of information Your Honour has seen within many UN reports, international reports, again, without specific identities or specific lead information that presents a -- a -- an exact conclusion being drawn. However, what it does show is a fact, a background, that these people were killed by somebody on a large scale and on the places and times indicated into the bar table as well as other significant crimes of a destructive nature being committed. We would not be in this position if we had had an opportunity over years to investigate and produce statements from people who provided an alpha to omega conclusion. In the circumstances of this litigation, such a conduct is simply not open to us; it's not possible. And the Trial Chamber would be meeting us straight away with, Well, what's going on here? This is totally unnecessary use of resources if you're going to conduct your litigation like that. All this information comes from the materials of the Prosecution. None of it's our materials. They are the people who have been, for many years, on the ground in the region and have collected the data. And, in our submission, it shows a -- a valid position by us in relation to the issue as to one of revenge by the local population. Again, and the note that I've just been given, because identities are not at issue here. It's the places, where they are falling within the area of the indictment. And as I said, we wouldn't be able to prove all this and set about erecting a Defence whereby we take a thousand, two thousand witness statements from local people detailing what had happened by then. The Court will know that's a simple impossibility. The best we can do with this kind of evidence, which is not unreasonable on our part, in my submission, is put together what is there that shows a picture. And for our purposes, we're not concerned whether these were committed by Serbian forces or -- or Serbian civilians. It's the fact that that they were happening in this region against Croats and in general terms at that time from 1991 to 1995. And, in our submission, what we've done here, having excluded many documents on the way and providing what we see as very concrete information about these reports, is adequate, it's relevant, it's -- it's evidence that the Court is able to receive and is of probative value in the terms of the larger issue, which is the basis for this bar table submission. And, in our submission, it is very unfair that, at this stage, when the last evidence was heard yesterday, that, suddenly, Mr. Carrier comes up with an objection to it that has not been voiced over two months. Previously, we dealt with this matter very amicably for the first bar table submission. We have submitted other details. We have a vast schedule from something called batch 14 which contain many specific allegations which came from interviews taken after these events by NGOs but weren't in the form of witness statements which the -- Mr. Waespi said he couldn't accept because none -- none of this was able to be investigated by them. We've had to abandon all that. And all those places were ones known to me. I had seen them during my experience in the Milosevic case. I was familiar with the places: Cviljane, Cetina, and these other places, and it rang a bell that there were things out there that could be of assistance to us on this particular issue. In my submission, it's very unfair for a one-eyed approach to be adopted on this kind of evidence and thereby disadvantage the Defence from what is a valid submission on the evidence, trying to keep this case totally focussed on -- on the Prosecution perspective of the events. This is far wider than the Martic Judgement. There are other aspects of the evidence which we were familiar with. We've had to abandon that. And we are trying to get information that is evidence that is probative and relevant to the Trial Chamber on this general issue, and we think Mr. Carrier's late edition into this issue and taking this position is very unfair on us because it wrong-foots us at the last moment. What do we do about it now? Given years ago, we could have taken steps to deal with this kind of issue, but that has not something that has been open to us. I only had six months to prepare this case and spent my time on the Prosecution case. This was something that came up as we went along and became an issue that we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Carrier, one issue raised by Mr. Kay was that in two month you didn't say anything and that it's -- you didn't respond, and that you now take a position which Mr. Kay considers not to be in line with an earlier position taken by the Prosecution on bar table submissions on events which took place before the indictment period. And the other one is that he says, Well, we're not proving exactly what happened. But what we are doing, we are establishing that apparently events took place which resulted in reports, et cetera, which give an overall picture, which -- which may have affected the minds of those who may have committed or have allegedly committed crimes at a later stage. That's basically what Mr. Kay tell us. So could I have on the two elements a brief response, if you want to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you, Mr. President. On the first point, in fact, it's completely consistent with our prior position with the first bar table motion by Mr. Kay. He originally filed six motions, the Prosecution had an issue with all the underlying evidence, and in fact the -- that first bar table submission was made up solely of portions of the Martic Judgement itself which was what the issue was. So this is an issue which we've raised consistently with Mr. Kay over and over with regard to the underlying documents. So it certainly isn't something new for him to consider. With regard to the second aspect, again, the Prosecution's position is that the Martic Judgement itself satisfies those grounds, if it's simply that there were crimes committed during that period in the Krajina against the Croatian or Croat population. That's in the Martic Judgement, and we can stipulate to that. And we have already done that with the first bar table motion, so it certainly isn't something new for Mr. Kay to consider, or -- that's something that I've simply raised today, something that the Prosecution's consistently brought to his attention over and over, including the batch 14 statements which he just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is intending to admit these bar table documents into evidence but would give an opportunity to the OTP to fill in the -- to fill in a comment column, if they wish to do so. If you say, All our comments and our objections are sufficiently set out in the oral submission, Mr. Carrier, then, of course, there is no need to further wait. But if you would say, Well, if the Chamber would admit that, then at least we would like to fill in the column and say this is in Austria rather than in any other place, or that person died already in 1953, or whatever. I don't know. But do you wish to have an opportunity, such an opportunity, if the Chamber would decide to admit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's fine. I think our position is clearly stated on the record, and there's no need to fill in the column which -- the purpose of which was to have the record clear on the Prosecution's position with respect to each of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber admits into evidence the 11 documents appearing in the bar table submission by the Cermak Defence related to the Rule 68 disclosure from the Prosecution's concerning crimes against Croats before Operation Storm. Mr. Registrar, would you please be so kind to prepare a list of -- a range of numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit numbers to be assigned to Cermak Defence second Rule 68 bar table submission would be D2147 throughout and including D2157. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The individual documents will be linked to the numbers in a further list to be prepared by the -- by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we received the spreadsheet, I think, through an e-mail. It should be formally filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. We were asked to put it to the Trial Chamber, at this stage, in that way. But we will do a proper filing. I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one item -- well, as a matter of fact, two items left for after a break, which we'll take soon. The one is a decision on the one remaining document out of the 92 which is MFI'd, whether the Chamber -- the handwritten report by Mr. Sacic which was then transcribed in an official report; that's one. The second is closure of the evidentiary phase of the case and further scheduling. We'll deal with that after the break. But I would like to know whether there are any other matters the parties would like to raise on this housekeeping session. If there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one matter. Witness 86's statement exhibited under seal, P487. He affirmed the B/C/S translation, of course, because he didn't read English, and the B/C/S translation needs to be -- have certain revisions made to it in terms of its accuracy. A schedule has been provided to the Prosecution on -- on this, and that is a matter, in hand. It comes around at this late stage as one is reviewing the evidence and B/C/S speakers, obviously, use the B/C/S content of the document. And that is a matter that the Trial Chamber should receive. I should imagine it is capable of agreement between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's no need to discuss it. It's a matter of, again, replacing translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think I gave the guidance already for how to deal with replacement of translations. That if there is an agreement between the parties on the matter, that it should be informally sent to the Registrar. The Chamber will look at it, the Chamber will grant permission to replace, and that at the very end we'll have a list of all those translations which were replaced since the -- since the hearings were concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. By and large this is a system that works very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then is there any other matter the Chamber would expect the parties to raise after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, one, let's say, tiny matter. It relates to the documents that the Markac Defence was trying to introduce into the evidence via bar table submission. And in that circumstances, Markac Defence contacted the OTP in March of this year. This is the document that depicts the surrender of 21 Kordun Corps after the -- completing Operation Oluja. And we thought that this document is both relevant and of probative value. And although we are aware that we tried to introduce this document after the closing of Defence case, it is our submission that Chamber is entitled to enter into the evidence every document that could be in the interests of justice and which could be relevant and of probative value. It is our position, then, this is the document that we are talking about. And to be precise, this is 3D00314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll forgive me for not having immediately a clear picture of what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a document about surrender of 21st Kordun Corps of the Army RSK on 9th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A huge amount of the weaponry and soldiers had been surrendered to the Croatian forces on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- I must honestly admit that I have -- you have now set out what the document is about, I have no clear recollection on how you tried to introduce it. I also do not know what the position of the Prosecution was in relation to that. So I have no clear picture of the procedural history of what is now raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no procedural history on the record. It's a document that the Markac Defence sought to admit to the bar table, and they have approached us to do so. And our position is consistent with the position we have taken in the past, that that document should have been tendered during the Defence portion of the case if that was what was the intention of the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what we're talking about is a document which has not been tendered in any way at all but which has been the subject of discussions between the parties, whether, if a bar table submission would be made, whether the Prosecution would object to that. I think I earlier said something about exceptionally to be admitted once the case is closed. So, therefore, the appropriate procedural way would be to -- I'm not saying that I'm encouraging you to do it, but if the Prosecution seems to oppose, then the only possible avenue would be to make it a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to add a little depth to this. We did not really get any kind of a response until repeatedly about this document, so obviously that's the reason we're bringing it up to the Chamber now because had we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what now happens and -- and when I earlier said I have no clear recollection, I don't know exactly where we are, what the procedural history of this is, then I was relieved by your answer that it was not on the record yet so that still my memory is -- knows where I rightly do not remember anything because nothing was ever said about it. Now, what I would like to avoid is that we now raise matters which are not formally introduced, which are not in any way on the record, and explain why, who responded, at what moment, late, early, what the relevance of the document is. Of course, the Chamber, under normal circumstances, if we're talking about these documents, we know what it is, we have an opportunity to look at it, we have detailed information as to why -- whether it's mainly for procedural reasons or for other reasons, I would suggest - but let me just consult with my colleagues for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I emphasise that I earlier said that only in exceptional cases the Chamber would allow new evidence or more evidence to be produced once the Defence case was closed. Keep that in mind. And if you deem it fit to make a bar table submission at this stage of the proceedings, then please explain why it is that the Chamber should not miss this document. And then we'll hear from the Prosecution, and we'll decide on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. We'll file it; it's one document. It's not -- it's a one-page document. So we will file it, and we'll try to file it today, and we'll see where it goes from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, at the same time, the Prosecution -- just as I said, the Defence should be aware of that only in exceptional circumstances. At the same time, the Prosecution could consider what exactly is at stake, to what extent this one document would totally overturn the situation in this courtroom. Let's try to be practical as well. No other matters to be expected. Then, after the break, we'll certainly further deal with the closure of the evidentiary phase of the case and further scheduling, and most likely we will give a decision on this one document out of the 92, which is marked for identification. We'll have a break, and we will resume at a quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I first would like to deliver the decision on the document which was MFI'd this morning, that's D2109, where the Prosecution had withdrawn its objections as to the provenance. D2109 is admitted into evidence. Another item which I did not announce before the break but I couldn't do so because it's a filing of today and I just wasn't aware of it, that is, the joint stipulation regarding the foundation of exhibits P319 and P757. I don't know whether the -- it's a joint stipulation by the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution. What about the other parties joining in this stipulation or not joining in the stipulation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll have to take a quick look at it. I know it came today. I was -- I am aware of it, but we'll let the Court know very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we make an arrangement that if we have not heard from the other Defence teams by, well, let's say by next week, Tuesday, that that silence is to be interpreted as joinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will join. I just -- I was aware of it; I just saw it again. We will join in the stipulation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, it is about who provided a certain exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just catching up on it. Your Honour -- if Your Honour gives me a few seconds, we can deal with this now, with the Court's leave. Your Honour, we can join this, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this has now become a joint stipulation between all parties, which is, for me, a reason to take you back to -- which is the non-admission of -- what was 65 ter number 7667, that is, the Subota stipulation, which was also a stipulation between the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution that no activities had been developed since August 1995 and that only in 2006 that case continued or was given any follow-up. There, the other parties did not join in this stipulation. The Chamber has decided that it will not admit into evidence the entire case file which mainly deals with what happens after 2006 exhumation, 2007, witnesses, et cetera. For very practical reasons, the Chamber may reconsider that decision of non-admission for matters which, of facts at the time - which is different from what we just had, which is who delivered a certain document. But if we're talking about facts at the time, that is, what happened between 1995 and 2006, the Chamber may have huge problems in Judgement drafting. Not to say that this will be a central element in the Judgement; I don't take it. But if we have to -- if we want to rely on one document or if we want to rely on the stipulation, then it creates a lot of technical problems for us to deal with one party and with the other parties and how to resolve that. And then it depends on whether the matter only affects one party or whether it affects all the parties. It is also difficult for the Chamber to forecast what problems that would give us. And, therefore, where the matter seems to be relatively simple, I went through the case file during the last break where we have a clear starting point which limits itself to August 1995, photographs taken, and then we see that there is new -- there is a case file with a number, which, as we know from Mr. Bajic, is a 06 number, that is, a file being opened in 2006; and then from the logic from what you see there, what reference is made to early investigative measures, if you look at what they intend or what they are asking for to be further investigated, that it seems - again without giving any final judgement on that - it seems that the stipulation between the parties is in every way supported by the material the Prosecution intended to tender, if there would be no stipulation. Now, the Chamber may find itself, if it's a stipulation between some parties only, may find itself later in problems and, therefore, urges both the Cermak Defence and the Markac Defence to consider whether there is a way to join that stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we talked about it over the break, and we decided to join the stipulation. So just to inform the parties and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you say "we" ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Meaning the Markac Defence, among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Cermak Defence, if you want more time, Mr. Kay, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could just follow it through, Your Honour, and have a look at it, and then we will be able to tidy this up, I'm sure, this morning. We don't want to cause any problems for the Trial Chamber, if we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now come to the next item which is the closure of the evidentiary phase of the case. And after that we'll deal with further scheduling. The hearing of evidence in the case of the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al is closed, but I make the following reservations, exceptions to that. First of all, we most likely will hear from Mr. Kay on the stipulation on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right; that activity just then was related to that. And I have been assured it's a stipulation we can also lend our support to. And that is agreed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Somewhat relieved now, I continue with the closure of the hearing of evidence in the case of the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al. I, however, make one exception for a bar table submission still expected today from the Markac Defence. Whether that leads to admission into evidence is another matter, but at least that is understood, that we'll receive and later decide on such a motion. And that's, therefore, exempted from the closure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- and that would be one document about the Kordun Corps; that's how we understood it. Now, there was still a couple of matters pending which have not been decided. As far as the Chamber, at this moment, can oversee, it does not except and even finds it a bit difficult to imagine that those pending issues where decisions are still to be taken would create a situation in which the parties would seek to present further evidence. We do not expect that. But you have not read our decisions. We have not seen any applications to that extent, but just for you to know that the Chamber doesn't expect that. But if it happens, then we'll consider it, what the consequences are; first, of our decision, and, second, then, what that decision or those decisions have triggered you in terms of making applications. But, we, at this moment, have difficulties imagining that that would lead to hearing further evidence. The same thing - and I think the Gotovina Defence has already made a reservation in that respect - there are a few matters pending before the Appeals Chamber. There, it's far more difficult for us to forecast or to know whether the decisions to be taken by the Appeals Chamber would create any situation which would have an impact on evidence already heard or still to be heard or whatever. We do not know. If decisions will be delivered by the Appeals Chamber, the Chamber will, in relation to whatever decision will be taken, will carefully consider whether or not this should have any consequences for the closure of the case or in any other way have any consequences for the proceedings before this Trial Chamber. And it goes without saying that parties, of course, can make submissions once we have seen such decisions. We just don't know them. It's still to be seen. That is -- these are two observations in relation to the closure of the hearing of evidence in this case. Any further comments on what I just said? Then the last item on my agenda is scheduling. The Chamber will deliver, soon, a decision on the final brief word extension requests. In this decision, we intend also to further set out scheduling such as deadlines for filing final briefs, dates of hearing closing arguments, and times allocated to present closing arguments. The Chamber has in mind to receive the final briefs in early July and hear the closing arguments soon after the summer recess. The Chamber would like to inquire with the parties what they expect in this respect and whether the Chamber should keep in mind any scheduling conflicts that may exist. So, therefore, having given a glance on what you could expect from us - early July, final briefs; after the recess, closing arguments - whether there are any further comments, comments, or observations by the parties. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, early July, looking at the calendar on my watch, that would imply to me three weeks. That would be too short a time, in my submission, given that we're just finishing evidence. A lot of my attention has had to be diverted in the last few weeks, and particularly -- in the last few months, in fact, with the Judges' witness, re-opening the case. And about three or four weeks for me to pay attention to what the rest of my team have been working on and to also write several sections myself is going to be too much of a challenge. I would ask the Court for a mid-July date. Because I -- I can just feel that that is too short a period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. And if I could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you don't have to apologise for putting your position before the Chamber, Mr. Kay. There is never a reason to apologise for what you say is hard work to be done. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, and early July, of course, is a bit of a flexible expression, which was -- Let me first hear from Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only conflict I have - I have made the Chamber aware, through informal communications, about an issue that it looks like it's not going to affect, for me, the briefing. Shortly after the recess, from the 17th to the 22nd of August, I am occupied in the States. Other than that, I have absolutely no August conflicts. So I wanted to let the Chamber know about that for me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that would be relevant for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Closings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that recess and the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... closing arguments --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Recess ends the 15th, but I think this Chamber has announced it will not sit in the week starting the 15th. Whether we announced it or not, we will not sit that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So the 17th through the 22nd, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the 15th is a Monday, the 17th would be Wednesday up to and including that weekend after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That week, we'll not sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any problems with the proposed schedule. I. Did wish to raise one matter which arose at the 98 bis hearings, and we'd ask the Chamber to keep this in mind in scheduling. The Chamber, in the 98 bis proceedings, set out a procedure whereby the Prosecution got a certain block of time and then all three Defences teams received an equal amount of time. But as it turned out, the Prosecution's arguments did not exactly break out into spending 33 per cent of its time with respect to each accused, which result in a situation that came up where the Markac Defence was kind enough to give some of its time to the Gotovina Defence to be able to respond. At the moment, I'm not exactly sure how to deal with the issue. But in terms of scheduling, we would appreciate some flexibility in terms of being able to respond to the Prosecution's arguments. That depends on, of course, how the Prosecution argues in its final argument, to avoid a situation where three hours are spent on one accused and one hour are spent -- is spent on two other accused. And I just wanted to bring that to the Chamber's attention right now, that depending on how the Scheduling Order breaks out and what happens in final argument, we may ask for some flexibility in that respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one last thing, Mr. President. I should have told Mr. Misetic this - we chatted about it - but, of course, we have no problem with the proposed schedule as requested by Mr. Kay. In our motion, with regard to the word limit, we did ask for some alternative remedy, should the Chamber consider granting the OTP 's request in any regard. And that would divert from the simultaneous filing of briefs to allow the Defence to take an additional two weeks after the filing of the OTP's brief and whatever information they have to allow to us to respond to that. So in taking the scheduling into consideration, I just wanted to bring there to the Court's attention. I know we just filed that this morning and I know it's rather recent and I'm not certain if my learned friends have had the opportunity to see that, but that's certainly in our filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I -- I think if you would ever have another trial, I would invite you to invite -- to inform the Court at every session what filings are to be expected in the two hours -- the first two hours of the session so that we can quickly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we had until noon time to file it, and so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, I'm -- you've got to know me a little, I think, by now that it's not serious criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, just so the Chamber knows, I know the Chamber stated that it would render a decision soon on the motion to extend the word limit, but we have -- I have only briefly looked at the motion of the Gotovina -- well, its response, and I guess what we view as a motion, as it's seeking also relief. So we will file today a request for leave to respond to that -- to that motion. We'll hope to file that today, and then we'll try to file it as soon as possible after that. In terms of the scheduling, we, as well, have been involved in these Chamber witnesses and the last witnesses obviously. So we would join in Mr. Kay's proposal of a mid-July date for final briefing. But, of course, we -- we leave it to the Chamber, although early July is quite -- is quite a wide range, so as soon as we can have some clarity on what the Chamber intends, we would -- and we would have a preference for the middle of July as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Is there any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter on the closing arguments after the final briefs are in, Your Honour. I have a domestic request and that is that we can have a summer holiday as well in this, that after we file Court factors in for us, the fact that some of us do need a holiday. And working over another summer holiday, after the last previous years, is -- is not too attractive back home. If I can put it that way. If the Court would bear in mind that there others who expect us to have a holiday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I'm fully aware of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- since my youth, that the text of Cliff Richard's "Summer Holiday" is with me. But to be very practical, would you -- I mean, you file a final brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's say, July. Then we will have -- you will have to prepare for final arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, where did you have in mind -- would you have -- and how much time - not to say that we're granting everything but to be -- would you say, Well, I'd like to have, well, let's say, the two last week, end of July, before we start. Or is it that you say, Make the final arguments as early as possible so that September is still available for holidays? And it's not -- I learned at home that I have to be very practical in this matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, we are tied in with school holidays. That's -- that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is this the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have three weeks' holiday. So if we have the last week of July or two weeks of August, however the Court configures the break, that we keep that as a break. And then the time for response to -- for preparations for the closing argument can be factored after that. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then, of course, the Chamber would need a further indication as to how much time you think you would need for that. If you say, Well -- if we say, final briefs, early July; the final argument after the recess, then we have -- well, let's say, if early July would be after the first week of July, then it would be approximately five weeks, which we had scheduled as time in between. We did not express ourselves on whether you would be in your -- on the beach or in your law firms during that period of time. Do you think that's enough for holiday and being in your offices, or would you say, No, for having our families with us for two weeks. How much time would you then consider you would still need to further prepare?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think a preparation time in response of three weeks is -- is enough. And that's manageable. We all know the case. But whatever time is, if we can have the three-week holiday and then three weeks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- but I'm asking this because I'm wondering where there is a problem. Let's just assume that we would follow you and say mid-July. Then two weeks would remain in July which are school holidays weeks, I take. Then I said we're not sitting in the week of the 15th, which brings us already to the 22nd of August, a Monday, in that week, at least, which would create the initial three weeks. So, therefore, I'm -- I'm asking myself: What -- if -- if we would you give you the mid-July option and if we would certainly not resume before the 22nd of August, where you say you would need two weeks for the family and three weeks for a -- preparing, that's five weeks, which is, I would say, more or less safe-guarded in what is projected at this moment, if we would follow your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That week of the 15th of August which is a court blank week, I know Mr. Kuzmanovic has got commitments. I have got lecturing commitments that week as well for -- at Salzburg, two days. I know others are going to be there as well. I'm doing two days, though, which was decided a year ago that I would, having missed the last two summers for Mr. Triffterer -- Professor Triffterer. So, I in a way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you say ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... a week after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A couple of more days would -- because now it becomes more clear. You need two weeks for the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You need three weeks for preparations of which some days were stolen by Professor Triffterer, and whether we can provide compensation for that theft. Is that -- now it becomes clear to me where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it is a public record. My apologies already to Professor Triffterer. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I offer a possible resolution to -- for all parties, that we just have oral arguments September 1st or 1 September, if that's satisfies the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well see. You are very generous for Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I just figured without going into the dicing and splicing of respective schedules and people having to be various locales that might be the most -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, we'll consider that. Most important for us was where there would be real problems. We have heard from Mr. Kay where his real problems are. We heard from Mr. Kuzmanovic where his real problems are. Mr. Kehoe, as always, you have no real problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's appreciated. And you give a suggestion. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I prefer not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to prolong this, but I -- what Mr. Kehoe suggested as a possible alternative is agreeable. That Monday, the 30th of August -- the 30th of August is a Monday; September 1st is a Wednesday. So, that -- that range fits with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider it. We have been, for quite a while, together in court, normally with the accused; today without the accused. I would express the appreciation of the Chamber for the cooperative attitude we usually have found. It's not uncommon that small frictions now and then arise as well. We have dealt with them in such a way that we still -- that I still can say that, finally, the Chamber considered the atmosphere in the courtroom over these many many months the type of atmosphere one would desire. There are still hard times to come. The parties will have to do a lot the work. The Chamber will have to a lot of work. To the extent I ever was at moments a bit unfair to you, I still hope that you will forgive me for that. And we'll resume at the date which you will find in the decision, which includes scheduling. We stand adjourned, sine die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: sine die

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.57 a.m.,
